query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: If a eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies is subjected to staged warm/cold deformation (at ~600–700 °C) followed by partial annealing (at ~600–800 °C), then the resulting refined lamellar microstructure with stabilized sub-lamellar boundaries will simultaneously increase yield strength by at least ~10% and raise total tensile elongation beyond 10% at room temperature, compared to the as-cast lamellar-colony baseline, by suppressing microcrack initiation at internal boundaries and promoting more uniform deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (dual-phase lamellar colonies).
generation.intervention: Perform moderate-temperature forging or rolling (600–700 °C) with total strain ~2–3, followed by a brief partial annealing (600–800 °C) to disrupt and refine lamellar colonies without full recrystallization.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined lamellae with stabilized dislocation substructures and smaller, crack-arresting boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Partial transformation and controlled refinement of the lamellar structure reduce stress concentrations and enhance cohesive boundary strength, retarding early microcrack formation and enabling improved uniform ductility while raising the yield stress.
generation.predicted_outcome: At room temperature, yield strength ≥10% higher and total elongation >10% relative to the unmodified lamellar baseline.
generation.baseline: Unprocessed as-cast alloy with coarse lamellar colonies, prone to microcracking and brittle fracture at low tensile strains.
generation.boundary: Refinement requires careful temperature–time control. Overlong or excessive annealing coarsens lamellae, degrading the beneficial microstructure. Alloy compositional variations may also affect achievable strength–ductility combinations.
generation.uncertainty: Exact tensile property improvements depend on alloy chemistry and precise thermal/mechanical parameters. Further replication is required across different EHEAs and processing routes.

falsification_experiment.design: Process an as-cast EHEA sample using the staged warm/cold deformation plus partial annealing, then measure room-temperature tensile properties alongside an unprocessed control.
measurements: Comparative yield strength (from true stress-strain curves) for processed vs. baseline EHEA.
Elongation to failure via uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature, for processed vs. baseline EHEA.
Electron microscopy to confirm partial lamellar refinement and sub-lamellar boundary stabilization.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed sample’s yield strength does not rise by ≥10% or if the total elongation remains below 10% under the same testing conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. In the present study, the as-cast HEAs were subjected to cold rolling and subsequent annealing treatment (800, 900, and 1000 °C) to adjust the microstructures and tensile properties. This treatment process resulted in the partial recrystallization, full recrystallization, and grain coarsening with increasing the annealing temperature. decision.trend: Early work (PMC4145285) introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase lamellar (fcc/B2) microstructure showing good strength and moderate ductility at room temperature. Subsequent efforts (PMC6353877) refined these lamellae via tailored thermo-mechanical processing to yield ultrafine grains, improving the strength–ductility balance. Later developments (PMC6687781) employed severe plastic deformation (cryo-rolling plus warm-rolling) to produce mixed nanocrystalline and lamellar regions, achieving even higher strength levels (~2 GPa) but still with modest ductility (8%). Despite these innovations, microcrack initiation at internal boundaries remains a key unsolved challenge, causing brittleness under room-temperature tensile loading.
decision.unsolved: Although various thermo-mechanical pathways have improved strength and ductility relative to the as-cast lamellar-colony baseline, the presence of numerous internal interfaces and phase boundaries still leads to microcrack formation and catastrophic fracture at room temperature. Current strategies have not fully resolved the trade-off between high strength and adequate room-temperature tensile ductility in these eutectic high-entropy alloys.
decision.lever: A staged warm/cold deformation process (e.g., moderate-temperature forging or rolling at ~600–700 °C) followed by partial annealing to partially disrupt and refine lamellar colonies. Key processing parameters include a total strain of ~2–3 in the warm/cold deformation step and a brief anneal at a sufficiently low temperature (~600–800 °C) to stabilize dislocation substructures while avoiding coarsening of the lamellae.
decision.why: Existing studies highlight that refining the lamellar colonies and introducing heterogeneous structures can improve ductility through crack-arresting boundaries and reduced stress concentrations (PMC6353877, PMC6687781). A staged warm/cold deformation plus partial annealing strategy can generate stabilized sub-lamellar regions and finely tailored interfaces that impede microcrack formation. To test this hypothesis, one would compare tensile properties of an as-cast baseline EHEA and the new processed microstructure. If the refined lamellar microstructure does not simultaneously enhance yield strength (e.g., by at least 10%) and increase total elongation (e.g., >10%), the hypothesis that staged warm/cold deformation plus partial annealing can mitigate room-temperature brittleness would be falsified.
